newsitem.title: UK: Analysts watch for signs of rival Clyde bid.
newsitem.headline: Analysts watch for signs of rival Clyde bid.

text.p: Gulf Canada Resources' raised 120 pence per share bid for Britain's Clyde Petroleum Plc met with a cautious response from analysts on Tuesday, with shareholders advised to wait and see if a rival bid emerged.
However, there was consensus that Gulf's increased offer, valuing Clyde at 494.6 million stg, was not a clean knock-out.
"If that had been the opening offer it might have been different," said Credit Lyonnais Laing analyst Jurjen Lunshof, adding "I don't think it's enough."

With Clyde's share price resolutely stuck at the 120 pence offer level in Tuesday morning trading, analysts said it seemed to be pulled two ways - by the possibility of another bid emerging and the suspicion that "one or two large shareholders" might accept Gulf's offer.
An analyst with a UK-owned brokerage who asked not to be identified said "I think I would recommend holding (the stock) on the possibility of another bidder."

But a bank analyst, who also asked not to be named, said: "It is quite finely balanced now. There are a few shareholders who control a majority of the shares and of those one or two have been dithering about what sort of level they would find acceptable. This has certainly caught their attention."
And he added that "the risk is that if the bid fails the share price could go back to 90 pence. (Gulf) are trying to capitalise on that fear and some people will be persuaded."

After years of cost-cutting the oil industry is flush with cash, which has encouraged hopes that a counter-bid for Clyde could emerge. Gulf Canada said earlier on Tuesday that there had been "not a sniff or a rumour" of another bidder.

But the UK brokerage analyst said another Canadian company could emerge as a rival, noting that "the Canadian market is being valued on cash-flow multiples and on that baisis Clyde doesn't look expensive."

There was some criticism of Gulf Canada's attempt to play to two different audiences, attacking Clyde's prospects to Clyde shareholders while justifying its offer as fair value to its own stockholders.
"The point is that first and foremost Gulf's whole approach has been based on rubbishing Clyde's reserves," said Lunshof.
"Only yesterday they were saying there was nothing to pay up for in in Clyde's asset base, so why should they raise it by 15 percent for something that they think is complete rubbish?"

Lunshof said an offer of 125 pence to 135 pence would be justified. But the bank analyst said the 120 pence offer "is just in the right sort of ball park." He said 125 pence, which was widely tipped before Gulf Canada's announcement, would have made Gulf's position more certain.

Lunshof said shareholders should support the status quo. "It is not unreasonable to back management in this situation when we have seen much fancier premiums in the (exploration and production) sector." And he added: "it is all about persuading shareholders, and I think they can."

Bu the UK-brokerage analyst said while Clyde "is not particularly expensive versus its peer group, I think there is a question mark over it" in terms of its ability to grow successfully through acquisition and "a perception for them to overcome in terms of exploration failure."
"This is a very good move for Gulf Canada," he added.
